parts.text: After Joshua’s death, Israel asks who should lead the fighting, and the LORD names Judah. Judah and Simeon join forces, defeat Canaanites, and capture Adoni-bezek, who acknowledges the justice of receiving treatment he once gave others. The chapter recounts victories around Jerusalem, Hebron, and Debir, including Othniel’s marriage to Achsah and her request for springs. Yet Judah cannot drive out the inhabitants of the valley because they have chariots of iron.

The house of Joseph captures Beth-el with information from a local man. Other tribes leave Canaanites in their territories, sometimes imposing tribute when they become stronger. Benjamin leaves Jerusalem’s Jebusites, and the Amorites force Dan into the hill country. The account repeatedly distinguishes territorial claims from complete obedience in removing the inhabitants.

chapters.title: Israel’s repeated cycle of apostasy and deliverance

parts.text: An angel of the LORD rebukes Israel for failing to remove the nations’ altars and for making covenants with them. Those peoples and their gods will remain as troubles and snares. Israel weeps and sacrifices at Bochim. The chapter recalls Joshua’s death and the faithful generation that knew the LORD’s works, followed by a generation that does not know him or those works.

Israel serves Baalim and Ashtaroth, provoking God to deliver them to plunderers and enemies. He raises judges who rescue them, but the people repeatedly turn aside and become worse after each judge dies. Their persistent covenant-breaking leads God to leave nations in the land as a test of whether Israel will walk in his ways.

chapters.title: Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar deliver Israel

parts.text: God leaves certain nations to test Israel and teach warfare to generations unfamiliar with it. The Israelites intermarry with them and serve their gods. Because they forget the LORD, they are subjected to Chushan-rishathaim of Mesopotamia for eight years. When they cry to God, he raises Othniel, upon whom his Spirit comes. Othniel defeats the oppressor, and the land rests forty years.

Israel again does evil, and Eglon of Moab subdues them for eighteen years. God raises Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, who carries tribute to Eglon and kills him with a concealed dagger during a private meeting. Ehud escapes, rallies Israel, and defeats the Moabites at Jordan’s crossings. The land rests eighty years. Shamgar later delivers Israel by killing six hundred Philistines with an ox goad.

After Ehud’s death, Israel again sins and suffers under Jabin and his commander Sisera, who has nine hundred iron chariots. Deborah, a prophetess and judge, summons Barak to gather men from Naphtali and Zebulun. He will go only if she accompanies him. She agrees but announces that a woman will receive the honor of Sisera’s defeat. The LORD routs Sisera’s forces, and Barak destroys his army.

Sisera flees on foot to Jael’s tent, trusting the peace between Jabin and her husband Heber. She welcomes him, gives him milk, and covers him. While he sleeps, she drives a tent nail through his head. Barak arrives, and she shows him the dead commander. Israel grows stronger until Jabin is destroyed.

chapters.title: Deborah and Barak sing of victory

parts.text: Deborah and Barak praise the LORD and the people who willingly offered themselves. Their song recalls insecurity in Israel before Deborah arose and celebrates God’s majestic advance. It honors participating leaders and tribes while reproaching those who remained with flocks, ships, or distant settlements instead of joining the struggle. Zebulun and Naphtali are commended for risking their lives.

The song describes the battle against Canaan’s kings, with the stars fighting against Sisera and the river Kishon sweeping the enemy away. Meroz is cursed for failing to help, while Jael is blessed for killing Sisera. His mother is pictured waiting and imagining plunder, unaware of his death. The song asks that God’s enemies perish and his lovers shine in strength. The land rests forty years.

Israel’s sin brings seven years of devastating Midianite raids. A prophet explains that they have disobeyed the God who delivered them. An angel calls Gideon while he threshes wheat in hiding, commissioning him to save Israel. Gideon questions how his weak family can do this and asks for a sign. Fire consumes his offering, and he receives assurance of peace. He builds an altar to the LORD.

At God’s command, Gideon tears down his father’s Baal altar and grove and builds an altar to the LORD. Joash answers angry townsmen by saying Baal should defend himself. As enemy forces gather, the Spirit of the LORD comes upon Gideon, and he summons men. God grants his requested signs: first dew on the fleece alone, then dryness on the fleece while the ground is wet.

God reduces Gideon’s army so Israel cannot claim victory by its own strength. The fearful depart, and a drinking test leaves only three hundred men. To strengthen Gideon, God sends him with his servant into the enemy camp, where he hears a dream interpreted as a sign that God has delivered Midian into his hand. Gideon worships and returns encouraged.

He divides his men into three companies carrying trumpets, pitchers, and lamps. At his signal they break the pitchers, blow the trumpets, and shout. The LORD turns the enemy’s swords against one another, and the camp flees. Other Israelites join the pursuit. Ephraim seizes the Jordan crossings and captures and kills the Midianite princes Oreb and Zeeb.

chapters.title: Gideon’s final victory and a dangerous memorial

parts.text: Gideon appeases Ephraim’s anger at not being summoned earlier by praising its capture of Oreb and Zeeb. He pursues Zebah and Zalmunna with exhausted men, but Succoth and Penuel refuse food. After capturing the kings, he punishes those towns as threatened. Learning that the kings killed his brothers, Gideon executes them himself after his young son is afraid to do so.

Israel asks Gideon to rule as a hereditary leader, but he says the LORD shall rule. He requests gold earrings from the spoil and makes an ephod, which becomes a snare as Israel worships after it. Midian remains subdued, and the land rests forty years. Gideon has many sons, including Abimelech. After his death, Israel returns to Baal worship and forgets both God’s deliverance and Gideon’s kindness.

Abimelech persuades Shechem’s leaders to support his rule and kills his brothers, except Jotham, who escapes. Jotham addresses the city with a parable of trees choosing a king: useful trees decline, but the bramble offers doubtful shelter and threatens fire. He exposes Shechem’s betrayal of Gideon’s family and declares that, if their action is unjust, Abimelech and Shechem will destroy one another.

God sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem, bringing their shared bloodguilt to judgment. Rebellion under Gaal leads to fighting, and Abimelech destroys the city and burns people sheltering in a tower. At Thebez, a woman drops a millstone on his head; he orders his armorbearer to kill him. The account identifies both downfalls as the return of their wickedness upon them.

Tola judges Israel for twenty-three years after Abimelech, followed by Jair for twenty-two years. Israel again serves many foreign gods and forsakes the LORD. He gives them into the hands of the Philistines and Ammonites. Ammon oppresses the eastern tribes for eighteen years and crosses Jordan to attack Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim, leaving Israel sorely distressed.

The people confess their sin and cry for help. God recalls earlier deliverances and tells them to seek rescue from the gods they chose. They persist, put away foreign gods, and serve the LORD; he is grieved for their misery. As Ammon gathers and Israel camps at Mizpeh, Gilead’s leaders seek someone who will begin the battle and become their head.

Jephthah, driven out by his brothers because of his mother, becomes a leader in Tob. Gilead’s elders ask him to fight Ammon and agree to make him their head. He disputes the Ammonite king’s territorial claim by recounting Israel’s journey and conquest of Sihon’s Amorite land, arguing that Israel did not take Ammon’s land. The king refuses his message.

The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah. He vows that, if victorious, whatever comes from his house to meet him will belong to the LORD and be offered as a burnt offering. He defeats Ammon, but his only child, his daughter, comes out celebrating. After two months to mourn her virginity, she returns, and he does according to his vow. Israel’s daughters thereafter commemorate her annually.

chapters.title: Conflict with Ephraim and the later judges

parts.text: Ephraim angrily accuses Jephthah of excluding them from the Ammonite war and threatens to burn his house. He answers that he called for help but they did not save him. Fighting follows, and Gilead defeats Ephraim. At Jordan’s crossings, escaping Ephraimites are identified by their inability to pronounce Shibboleth. Forty-two thousand fall. Jephthah judges Israel six years and dies.

Ibzan judges for seven years and arranges marriages for his many sons and daughters outside his household. Elon the Zebulonite follows for ten years, then Abdon for eight. The chapter records their family details, periods of leadership, deaths, and burial places, carrying the account from Jephthah’s conflict toward the next period of oppression.

Israel again sins, and the LORD gives it to the Philistines for forty years. An angel tells Manoah’s barren wife that she will bear a son who will be a Nazarite from the womb and begin delivering Israel. She must avoid wine, strong drink, and unclean food, and no razor is to touch his head. Manoah asks God to send the messenger again, and the instructions are repeated.

Manoah offers hospitality, but the angel directs a burnt offering to the LORD. As the flame rises, the angel ascends in it. Manoah fears they will die after seeing God, but his wife reasons that God’s acceptance and promises show otherwise. She bears Samson, whom the LORD blesses, and his Spirit begins moving him.

Samson asks his parents to obtain a Philistine woman from Timnath as his wife. They object, not knowing that the occasion is of the LORD against the Philistines. On the journey, the Spirit strengthens Samson to tear apart a lion. Later he finds honey in its carcass, eats it, and shares some with his parents without explaining its source.

At the wedding feast, Samson challenges thirty companions with a riddle based on the lion and honey. They threaten his wife, who presses him until he reveals the answer and passes it to them. Samson recognizes their deception. Empowered by the Spirit, he kills thirty men in Ashkelon to pay the wager, then returns angrily to his father’s house. His wife is given to his companion.

chapters.title: Samson strikes the Philistines and is given water

parts.text: Samson returns to visit his wife, only to learn that her father has given her to another man. He captures three hundred foxes, ties firebrands between their paired tails, and releases them into Philistine crops. The Philistines burn his wife and her father in retaliation. Samson strikes them severely and withdraws to the rock Etam.

When Philistines threaten Judah, its men bind Samson to deliver him over. He permits this, but the Spirit of the LORD enables him to break the ropes and kill a thousand men with an ass’s jawbone. Exhausted by thirst, he calls upon God, who provides water and revives him. The chapter records that Samson judged Israel twenty years during Philistine domination.

Samson escapes a trap at Gaza by carrying away the city gates. Later Delilah, bribed by Philistine rulers, repeatedly asks the secret of his strength. After several false answers, her pressure brings him to disclose his lifelong Nazarite consecration and uncut hair. She has his hair shaved while he sleeps. He rises expecting his former strength, unaware that the LORD has departed from him.

The Philistines blind Samson and imprison him to grind, while his hair begins growing again. At a feast honoring Dagon, they bring him out for entertainment. Samson asks God for strength once more and pushes apart the supporting pillars, collapsing the building upon the rulers, crowd, and himself. His final act kills more than his earlier exploits. His family retrieves and buries him.

chapters.title: Micah’s private shrine and hired priest

parts.text: Micah admits taking his mother’s silver and returns it after hearing her curse. She dedicates silver to the LORD for a graven and molten image, which are installed in Micah’s house. He maintains a shrine with an ephod and teraphim and appoints one of his sons as priest. The account notes that Israel has no king and everyone does what seems right to him.

A young Levite from Beth-lehem travels seeking a place to live and comes to Micah’s house. Micah offers him wages, clothing, and food to serve as a father and priest. The Levite accepts and becomes like a son to him. Micah confidently expects the LORD’s favor because he now has a Levite as priest.

chapters.title: Dan captures Laish and adopts Micah’s idols

parts.text: Dan sends five men to find an inheritance. They lodge with Micah, recognize his Levite, and ask him to inquire of God about their journey. They find Laish quiet, prosperous, and isolated, then urge their brethren to take it. Six hundred armed Danites set out and arrive near Micah’s house.

The spies seize Micah’s images, ephod, and teraphim, and persuade the Levite to become priest to a whole tribe rather than one household. Micah protests but withdraws before their superior strength. The Danites attack Laish, kill its inhabitants, burn and rebuild it, and rename it Dan. They establish the stolen image and a hereditary priesthood, maintaining this worship while God’s house is at Shiloh.

A Levite goes to Beth-lehem to bring back his concubine, who has returned to her father. After repeated delays caused by hospitality, he leaves late and refuses to lodge in foreign Jebus, choosing Benjamin’s Gibeah instead. At first no one receives them, but an old man from Ephraim takes them into his house and provides for them.

Wicked men surround the house and demand the Levite for sexual abuse. The host offers women instead. The Levite puts his concubine outside, and the men abuse her through the night. She collapses at the door. In the morning he takes her away, cuts her body into twelve pieces, and sends them through Israel. The nation is appalled and calls for deliberation over an unprecedented outrage.

Israel gathers at Mizpeh, hears the Levite’s account, and demands that Benjamin surrender Gibeah’s offenders. Benjamin refuses and musters for battle. Israel seeks God’s direction, but suffers heavy losses in the first two engagements. The people weep, fast, and offer sacrifices before the LORD, with Phinehas ministering before the ark. God then promises victory on the next day.

Israel uses an ambush to draw Benjamin’s defenders away from Gibeah. The hidden force captures and burns the city, and the main army turns upon the pursuers. Benjamin is overwhelmingly defeated; only six hundred men escape to the rock Rimmon. Israel then destroys people, animals, and towns throughout Benjamin, turning the conflict into a near destruction of the tribe.

chapters.title: Israel seeks wives for the surviving Benjamites

parts.text: Israel mourns that one tribe is nearly lost, yet its men have sworn not to give daughters to Benjamin. They discover that Jabesh-gilead did not attend the national assembly and send an army to punish it under an earlier oath. Its inhabitants are killed except four hundred young virgins, who are given to the surviving Benjamites after an offer of peace.

Two hundred men still lack wives. The elders direct them to seize women dancing at the yearly feast in Shiloh, promising to answer their families’ complaints by arguing that the fathers did not voluntarily give them. Benjamin’s survivors rebuild their towns, and Israel returns to its inheritances. The book closes by repeating that, without a king, everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
